title: The prophets foretold the death of a man
source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἅπερ ἐν ὑποθέσει παρειλήφαμεν παραπλήσιά ἐστι ταῖς περὶ Ἰησοῦ προφητείαις. οὐ γὰρ προεῖπον αἱ προφητεῖαι θεὸν σταυρωθήσεσθαι, αἵτινές φασι περὶ τοῦ ἀναδεξαμένου τὸν θάνατον· „καὶ εἴδομεν αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν εἶδος οὐδὲ κάλλος, ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶδος αὐτοῦ ἄτιμον, ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων· ἄνθρωπος ἐν πληγῇ ὢν καὶ πόνῳ καὶ εἰδὼς φέρειν μαλακίαν.“ ὅρα οὖν (ὡς) σαφῶς ἄνθρωπον εἰρήκασι τὸν πεπονθότα ἀνθρώπινα. καὶ αὐτὸς ἀκριβῶς εἰδὼς Ἰησοῦς ὅτι τὸ ἀποθνῇσκον ἄνθρωπος ἦν, φησὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας αὐτῷ· „νῦν δὲ ζητεῖτέ με ἀποκτεῖναι, ἄνθρωπον, ὃς τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὑμῖν λελάληκα, ἣν ἤκουσα ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ.“ εἰ δέ τι θεῖον ἐν τῷ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν νοουμένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐτύγχανεν, ὅπερ ἦν ὁ μονογενὴς τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ὁ „πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως,“ ὁ λέγων· „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀλήθεια“ καὶ „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ζωὴ“ καὶ „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα“ καὶ „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς“ καὶ „ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβάς“· ἄλλος δή που ὁ περὶ τούτου καὶ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ λόγος ἐστὶ παρὰ τὸν περὶ τοῦ νοουμένου κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀνθρώπου. διόπερ οὐδ᾿ οἱ πάνυ ἁπλούστατοι καὶ λόγοις οὐκ ἐντεθραμμένοι ἐξεταστικοῖς Χριστιανοὶ εἴποιεν ἂν τεθνηκέναι τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἢ τὴν ζωὴν ἢ τὴν ὁδὸν ἢ τὸν ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καταβάντα ζῶντα ἄρτον ἢ τὴν ἀνάστασιν· φησὶ γὰρ ἑαυτὸν ἀνάστασιν εἶναι ὁ ἐν τῷ φαινομένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν διδάξας τὸ „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις.“ ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐδεὶς (οὕτως) ἐμβρόντητος ἡμῶν ἐστιν, ἵν᾿ εἴπῃ· τέθνηκεν „ἡ ζωὴ“ ἤ· τέθνηκεν „ἡ ἀνάστασις.“ ἦν δ᾿ ἂν τὸ τῆς ὑποθέσεως τοῦ Κέλσου χώραν ἔχον, εἰ ἐφάσκομεν προειρηκέναι τοὺς προφήτας τεθνήξεσθαι τὸν θεὸν λόγον ἢ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἢ τὴν ζωὴν ἢ τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἤ τι τῶν ἄλλων, ἅ φησιν εἶναι ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: But not even the things we took up (παραλαμβάνω) in hypothesis are like (παραπλήσιος) the prophecies about Jesus. For the prophecies did not foretell God would be crucified (σταυρόω), which say about the one who took up (ἀναδέχομαι) death: 'and we saw him, and he had no form (εἶδος) nor beauty (κάλλος), but his form dishonoured (ἄτιμος), failing (ἐκλείπω) beside the sons of men; a man being in a blow (πληγή) and toil (πόνος) and knowing to bear weakness (μαλακία).' See then how clearly they have called a man the one who suffered human things (ἀνθρώπινα). And Jesus himself, knowing precisely (ἀκριβῶς) that the dying thing was a man, says to those plotting against him: 'but now you seek to kill (ἀποκτείνω) me, a man who has spoken (λαλέω) to you the truth which I heard from God.' But if something divine (θεῖον) happened to be (τυγχάνω) in the man understood (νοέω) in respect of him, which was the only-begotten (μονογενής) of God and the 'firstborn (πρωτότοκος) of all creation (κτίσις)', the one saying 'I am the truth' and 'I am the life' and 'I am the door (θύρα)' and 'I am the way (ὁδός)' and 'I am the living bread (ἄρτος) having come down (καταβαίνω) from heaven'; surely (δή που) the account (λόγος) about this one and his essence (οὐσία) is other than that about the man understood in Jesus. Wherefore not even the very simplest (ἁπλοῦς) Christians, not nurtured (ἐντρέφω) in examining (ἐξεταστικός) arguments, would say the truth has died or the life or the way or the living bread come down from heaven or the resurrection (ἀνάστασις); for he says himself to be resurrection, the one who in the man appearing (φαίνομαι) in Jesus taught 'I am the resurrection.' But also none of us is so thunderstruck (ἐμβρόντητος) as to say: 'the life has died' or 'the resurrection has died.' The [matter] of Celsus's hypothesis would have had place (χώρα), if we said the prophets had foretold that God the Word (θεὸς λόγος) would die, or the truth or the life or the resurrection or some other of the things which the Son of God says he is.
pass_b_english: But not even the things we took up by way of hypothesis are like the prophecies about Jesus. For the prophecies did not foretell that God would be crucified. Of him who took death upon himself they say: “And we saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honour, falling short of the sons of men; a man stricken and in pain, and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:2–3). See, then, how plainly they have called a man the one who suffered human things. And Jesus himself, knowing exactly that what was dying was a man, says to those plotting against him: “But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from God” (John 8:40).

But if there was something divine in the man understood in him, namely the Only-begotten of God and “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), who says “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and “I am the life” (John 11:25), and “I am the door” (John 10:9), and “I am the way” (John 14:6), and “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51), then surely the account of him and of his essence is a different one from the account of the man understood in Jesus.

That is why not even the very simplest Christians, who have not been trained in critical reasoning, would say that the truth died, or the life, or the way, or the living bread that came down from heaven, or the resurrection. For he who, in the man seen in Jesus, taught the words “I am the resurrection” (John 11:25) says that he himself is the resurrection. Indeed, none of us is so witless as to say: “The life has died,” or “The resurrection has died.” Celsus’s hypothesis would have had some ground if we claimed that the prophets had foretold that God the Word would die, or the truth, or the life, or the resurrection, or any other of the things which the Son of God says he is.

choices.choice: Isaiah 53:2-3 is quoted from the Septuagint (ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων; the LXX adds πάντας), which differs from the Hebrew-based English text; ἐν πληγῇ ὢν καὶ πόνῳ rendered ‘stricken and in pain’. John 8:40 reads παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ where Origen has ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ; same sense. ‘I am the truth’ and ‘I am the way’ both come from John 14:6; ‘I am the life’ from John 11:25 or 14:6 (cited 11:25, where ‘the life’ stands beside ‘the resurrection’). ‘I am the door’ matches John 10:9 (also 10:7). John 6:51 is quoted word for word (ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβάς). (ὡς) and (οὕτως) are editorial supplements and are followed. ἐν τῷ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν νοουμένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ rendered ‘the man understood in him’, matching τοῦ νοουμένου κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀνθρώπου (‘the man understood in Jesus’); Origen distinguishes the man Jesus from the divine Word in him. ‘Only-begotten’ capitalised as a title of the Son. Truth, life and so on are kept lower-case as in the Gospel sayings; ‘God the Word’ capitalised.
ἐν πληγῇ ὢν καὶ πόνῳ: 'under a blow and in toil' (stiff) -> 'stricken and in pain'
ἐν τῷ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν νοουμένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ: 'the man understood to be in him' -> 'the man understood in him' ('to be' was added; now parallels 'the man understood in Jesus')
μονογενής as a title of the Son capitalised: 'the Only-begotten of God'
Translator note corrected: John 6:51 is quoted exactly, not loosely; John 8:40 ἀπό/παρά difference noted
Scripture checked: Isaiah 53:2-3 LXX, John 8:40, Colossians 1:15, John 14:6, John 11:25, John 10:9, John 6:51 all confirmed against the verse wording
